planting.note: Set out divisions or container plants in spring once soil has warmed, in any well-drained to moist soil in full sun to partial shade; 'Purple Showers' is a taller, sterile selection suited to mixed borders and mass plantings where the straight species would seed too freely.

directions: Grow 'Purple Showers' in any well-drained to moist garden soil in full sun to partial shade, spacing plants 18-24 inches apart to fill in as a dense border clump within a season. This is one of the older sterile-flowering selections of Mexican petunia developed to give gardeners the species' rich violet-purple, funnel-shaped blooms and nonstop summer-to-frost flowering without the aggressive rhizome spread and seed-borne invasiveness of unimproved seed-grown stock. Plants form upright, well-branched clumps to about 2 feet tall and tolerate heat, humidity, drought, and coastal salt exposure with minimal fuss once established. Cut the clump back hard in late winter where it dies to the ground, or shear by a third in midsummer to encourage a fresh flush of bloom on tidy new growth.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Ruellia simplex Cultivar Comparison
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Non-Invasive Mexican Petunia Cultivars

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown starts in spring in any well-drained to moist soil in full sun to partial shade; 'Bonita' stays compact and mounding, making it a good scale for foundation plantings and large containers.

directions: Site 'Bonita' in any well-drained to moist soil in full sun to partial shade, allowing 14-18 inches between plants for a full mounded clump. This compact Mexican petunia selection produces the same funnel-shaped, violet-purple flowers as the species on a smaller, denser frame than the wild form, making it easier to keep tidy in beds bordering lawns or natural areas. Each flower opens for a single day but is replaced continuously through the growing season, giving a steady show from spring through the first hard frost. Established clumps shrug off heat, humidity, and short dry spells; shear lightly after the first big flush to keep growth compact and encourage repeat bloom.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — Non-Invasive Mexican Petunia Cultivars
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Ruellia for Texas Landscapes

planting.note: Set out divisions or container plants in spring in any well-drained to moist soil in full sun to partial shade; 'Chi Chi' is grown for its clear pink flower color, a departure from the more common purple-flowered selections.

directions: Grow 'Chi Chi' in any well-drained to moist soil in full sun to partial shade, spacing clumps 18-24 inches apart. This selection carries soft pink, funnel-shaped flowers instead of the species' typical purple, opening in flushes over narrow, willowy foliage from late spring through frost, and is a favorite for gardeners who want the toughness of Mexican petunia with a softer color in cottage-style or pastel-themed beds. Like other named Ruellia simplex selections it flowers heavily on a single-day cycle but sets little to no viable seed, so it stays in place rather than colonizing nearby beds. It tolerates heat, humidity, and periods of drought once rooted in; cut back hard after a killing frost and again by a third in midsummer if stems become sparse at the base.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Ruellia simplex Cultivar Comparison

common_name: Susie Orange with Black Eye Vine
scientific_name: Thunbergia alata 'Susie Orange with Black Eye'

planting.note: Start seed indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost, nicking the hard seed coat or soaking overnight to speed germination, then transplant to a trellis, hanging basket, or fence after frost danger has passed.

directions: Start 'Susie Orange with Black Eye' indoors at 65-70F and transplant after last frost onto a small trellis, obelisk, or hanging basket where its twining stems can climb or cascade. This selection from the classic Susie seed strain reliably produces the bold, bright-orange, five-petaled flowers with a dark purple-black central throat that gave Black-Eyed Susan Vine its name, without the color variability of an open-pollinated mix. It flowers nonstop from early summer through the first frost and thrives in Gulf Coast heat and humidity that slow many other annual vines. Pinch young growth to encourage branching and deadhead spent flowers occasionally to keep the display fresh.
sources: Park Seed — Thunbergia alata 'Susie' series growing guide
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Annual Vines for Florida Gardens

planting.note: Start seed indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost after soaking overnight, and transplant to a trellis, fence, or basket once nights stay reliably above 50F.

directions: Grow 'Susie White' on the same schedule as other Black-Eyed Susan Vine selections, starting seed indoors and moving transplants to a trellis or hanging basket after frost. Its creamy-white petals surround the same dark, near-black central throat typical of the Susie strain, giving a crisp, high-contrast flower that reads well against dark foliage backdrops or in white-and-green moon gardens. Vines twine quickly to cover a small support and bloom continuously through the hottest part of the Gulf Coast summer with little more than routine watering. Provide consistent moisture during establishment and pinch tips early to build a fuller, more floriferous plant.
sources: Thompson & Morgan — Thunbergia alata 'Susie' series descriptions
Missouri Botanical Garden — Thunbergia alata plant profile

planting.note: Set out vegetatively propagated transplants after last frost onto a trellis, obelisk, or hanging basket in full sun to partial shade; this cultivar is typically sold as started plants rather than grown from seed.

directions: Plant 'African Sunset' after all danger of frost in full sun to partial shade, training the twining stems onto a trellis or letting them spill from a hanging basket. Unlike classic black-eyed forms of Thunbergia alata, this selection lacks the dark central eye and instead opens in warm apricot and rusty-orange tones that fade toward soft cream and pink as each flower ages, so a single plant shows several color phases at once. It blooms continuously from late spring through frost and handles Gulf Coast heat and humidity as well as any Thunbergia alata selection, needing only regular moisture and an occasional pinch to stay full and bushy. Because it is propagated vegetatively rather than from seed, plants are uniform in color pattern from batch to batch.
sources: Proven Winners — Thunbergia 'African Sunset' plant information
